summary: A country on the island of Ireland in the Atlantic that became independent from Britain in 1922, known for literature, Celtic music and St. Patrick's Day, and in recent years a major European technology hub.

ranking.name: Catholicism
ranking.description: After St. Patrick's mission in the 5th century, Christianity took root in Ireland; when Britain pushed Protestant reform in the 16th century, most Irish people held fast to Catholicism and, under the oppression of the Penal Laws, made their faith a part of national identity. After independence in 1922 the Catholic Church controlled most schools and hospitals, so it is still the largest religion today. The proportion has, however, continued to fall from about 95% in 1961.

ranking.name: No religion
ranking.description: From the 1990s scandals such as sexual abuse by Catholic clergy and the "Magdalene laundries" were revealed one after another, seriously damaging the church's prestige; at the same time the "Celtic Tiger" economic boom brought urbanization and the spread of higher education. In the 2022 census the number of non-religious people rose by about sixty percent from 2016, with the most among young people in cities such as Dublin.

ranking.name: Protestantism (Church of Ireland, etc.)
ranking.description: In the 16th–17th centuries Britain pushed the Reformation in Ireland and settled large numbers of English and Scottish Protestant migrants in the Ulster Plantation, forming the Anglican Church of Ireland and Presbyterian communities. At Partition in 1921 Protestants were mostly concentrated in the north, which became Northern Ireland, so the Protestants who remained in the Republic are only a minority, now found mostly in Dublin and the border counties.

ranking.name: Eastern Orthodoxy
ranking.description: After the EU's eastward enlargement in 2004, migrants from Eastern European countries such as Romania and Bulgaria came to Ireland to work in large numbers and brought Orthodoxy with them. Romanian, Russian and Greek Orthodox churches have been set up in Dublin and elsewhere, and the believers are mainly families of young migrant workers.

ranking.name: Islam
ranking.description: From the 1950s a small number of medical students from places such as South Africa and Malaysia formed a Muslim community in Ireland, and the first mosque was established in Dublin in 1976. After the economic prosperity of the 1990s, migrants and refugees from Pakistan, Nigeria and the Middle East increased, making Islam one of the fastest-growing minority religions.

religion.background: Tradition says St. Patrick came to Ireland to preach around AD 432; in the 6th–8th centuries Irish monasteries became centers of European learning, and monks even traveled to Scotland and the Continent to preach. In the 16th century King Henry VIII of England pushed the Reformation, but most Irish people refused to convert, and Britain thereafter used the Penal Laws to restrict Catholics' rights to land, education and political participation, so religion became tied to the national identity of "the Irish resisting British rule". After Catholic Emancipation in 1829 and the founding of the Irish Free State in 1922, the Catholic Church long dominated education and social policy. From the 1990s the scandals of sexual abuse by clergy came to light, and together with the economic boom and urbanization, society secularized rapidly, with referendums in 2015 and 2018 approving same-sex marriage and the legalization of abortion in turn.

language.official: Irish (the first official language) and English are the official languages.

ranking.name: English
ranking.description: English began to enter Ireland after the Norman invasion of the 12th century, and the British colonization and plantation policies of the 16th–17th centuries made English the language of administration, law and commerce. The Great Famine of the 19th century and the national schools (from 1831), which taught in English, led parents to switch to English so that their children could emigrate or make a living, and by the 20th century English had become the mother tongue of the vast majority.

ranking.name: Irish
ranking.description: Irish was once the language spoken across the whole island, but declined sharply under British rule and after the Great Famine. After independence the government made it a compulsory school subject, and about forty percent of the population say they can speak it, but those who use it daily outside school are only about 2%, concentrated in the Gaeltacht, the Irish-speaking areas of the west coast in Galway, Donegal, Kerry and elsewhere.

ranking.name: Polish
ranking.description: When Poland joined the EU in 2004, Ireland was one of the few countries to open its labor market immediately, and large numbers of young Poles came to work in construction and services, making Polish the second most commonly used home language in Ireland, with Polish shops and Masses to be seen in cities such as Dublin.

language.history: Irish belongs to the Celtic language family and had already developed a rich literature in the Middle Ages, and was even adopted by the Norman nobles who invaded in the 12th century. In the 16th–17th centuries Britain reconquered Ireland and pursued colonization, and English became the language of politics and commerce; the Great Famine of 1845–1852 caused about a million deaths and a million emigrants, and those hardest hit were precisely the Irish-speaking poor farmers of the west, so the language quickly collapsed. The Gaelic League was founded in 1893 to promote revival, after independence in 1922 Irish became a compulsory school subject, and in 1937 the constitution made it the first official language, but English remains the mother tongue of the vast majority.

ranking.name: Irish stew
ranking.description: A clear stew simmered from mutton (or neck of lamb), potato and onion, with carrot added in some households; the flavor is simple.
ranking.history: Irish stew originates in farmhouse cooking: shepherds stewed old sheep or cheap cuts such as the neck together with cheap root vegetables for a long time. After the 17th century the potato became the staple of the Irish poor, and the stew also made the potato its star, so it is often regarded as a microcosm of the potato and sheep-farming economy. Documents of the 19th century already treated it as a representative Irish dish, and today it almost always appears on St. Patrick's Day (March 17) and on pub menus.

ranking.name: Soda bread
ranking.description: A quick bread leavened with baking soda instead of yeast and with buttermilk added to make the dough rise, with a hard crust and a dense, slightly sour crumb.
ranking.history: In the 1830s–1840s baking soda (sodium bicarbonate) began to be sold in Ireland, which suited the low-gluten soft wheat grown in the local climate, flour that does not ferment well with yeast. Farm families could bake it in an iron pot over a peat fire, so it spread quickly. The round loaf is cut with a cross on top, which folk belief says is "to let the fairies out" or to ask for a blessing; in Northern Ireland it is often made as a flat "farl" cut into quarters.

ranking.name: Full Irish breakfast
ranking.description: Fried bacon, sausage, egg, black pudding and white pudding (blood sausage and oatmeal sausage), with baked beans, tomato, mushrooms and soda bread, and a pot of tea.
ranking.history: This hearty breakfast originated in the farm families' habit of needing lots of calories before going out to the fields at dawn, while the processed pork products come from the tradition of farm families slaughtering pigs in autumn and winter to preserve meat. Black pudding is made from pig's blood and oatmeal, a country food that wastes nothing. In the 19th–20th centuries it developed alongside the English full breakfast, and the distinctive features of the Irish version are white pudding and soda bread; today it is the signature breakfast of hotels and cafés and is also regarded as a family ritual at weekends or after a hangover.

ranking.name: Colcannon
ranking.description: Mashed potato mixed with chopped cabbage or kale, scallions and plenty of butter, with a creamy texture. A well is often made in the middle and filled with melted butter; it is a common side dish in autumn and winter.
ranking.history: The name Colcannon comes from the Irish "cál ceannann", meaning "white-headed cabbage". It appears in documents by the 18th century and is a home dish of the age after the potato became common. Traditionally it is eaten on Halloween eve (derived from the Celtic festival of Samhain), when people hide a ring, a coin or a thimble in it, and whoever gets it is said to be foretold marriage, wealth or being single; a 19th-century folk song, "Colcannon", also sings of this dish.

ranking.name: Boxty (potato pancake)
ranking.description: Raw grated potato is squeezed dry, mixed with mashed potato, flour and buttermilk and fried into a thin pancake, crisp outside and soft inside. It can be a breakfast with bacon, or rolled around a stew as a main dish.
ranking.history: Boxty comes from the Irish "arán bocht tí" (poor man's bread), is popular in the north-central counties of Leitrim, Cavan, Sligo and others, and is a product of the age of the potato staple in the 18th–19th centuries. The folk rhyme "Boxty on the griddle, boxty in the pan, if you can't make boxty, you'll never get a man" reflects that it was once a dish every housekeeper had to know. It was rarely seen for a while after the Great Famine, and in recent years has become a distinctive Irish dish again through the revival by restaurants.
